
The pseudo-static seismic coefficient represents the maximum horizontal acceleration ($\bar{a}_{h.max}$) expected in a failure wedge in slip potential and is obtained by averaging the horizontal (instantaneous) forces in the deformable sliding mass. The *horizontal* seismic coefficient, measured in units of $g$, is usually expressed in terms of the maximum ground acceleration $pga$ according to $k_{max}=k_h \ pga$. In pseudo-static slope stability analysis, the adoption of seismic coefficients $k<k_{max}$ combined with $FoS=1$ indicates that some residual displacements will be expected. There are a number of models in the literature that enable the estimation of the seismic coefficient $k_{max}$ based on the peak ground acceleration $pga$ and the geometry of the soil mass.The empirical model from @Bray2018, provides an estimate of residual displacements $D_n$ for different yield coefficients $k_y$ and intensity levels $Sa(T_d)$. The seismic coefficient $k_{max}$ is obtained for that value of the yield coefficient $k_y$ such that the (mean) residual displacements $\eta_D$ are less than or equal to a target displacement $D_a$ according to the following expression:

$$\mathrm{ln} \ k_{max} \approx a_0+a_1 \ \mathrm{ln} \ S_a(T_d)+a_2 \ +a_2 \ (\mathrm{ln} \ S_a(T_d))^2$$ {#eq-KMAX}

where $S_a(T_d)$ is the intensity level defined at the shifted period $T_d=1.3 T_s$, and $a_0,a_1,a_2$ are model parameters depending on the target displacement $d_a^*$, the peak-ground velocity $pgv$, the slope's fundamental period $T_d$ and the moment magnitude $M_w$ representative for the maximum considered seismic event. Seismic coefficients from this methodology are based on the condition of rigid plastic yielding deformation on a well-defined failure surface and therefore limited in terms of their application to compacted clayey embankments and dry or dense cohesionless soils that experience very little reduction in strength due to cyclic loading. The proposed methodology should not be applied in cases where embankments or their foundations are susceptible to liquefaction or strain weakening, as the residual displacements will be significantly underestimated.
